questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with multiple dome-shaped, pearly-white papules with central umbilication on the arms and trunk. Which molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV) genotype is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
opts: MCV-2
MCV-1
MCV-3
MCV-4
questions.exp: MCV-1 is the most dominant subtype worldwide, responsible for 76–98% of childhood infections globally and up to 98% of cases in the United States. MCV-2 is predominantly sexually transmitted in adults and immunosuppressed individuals. MCV-3 and MCV-4 are extremely rare subtypes.

questions.q: A 5-day-old premature male (32 weeks gestation, 1.2 kg) presenting with sepsis and severe hypothermia develops rapid-onset, diffuse, board-like induration of the buttocks, thighs, and calves over 24 hours. The skin is cold, rock-hard, non-pitting, and yellowish-white with purplish mottling. Palms and soles are spared. Histology shows fat necrosis with minimal inflammation and pathognomonic doubly refractile, needle-shaped crystals arranged radially within adipocytes. Which mechanism best explains the pathogenesis of this condition?
opts: High ratio of unsaturated to saturated fatty acids causing spontaneous lipid peroxidation
Autoimmune-mediated adipocyte destruction triggered by HLA-associated antibodies
Immature enzymatic lipolysis coupled with peripheral circulatory collapse causing crystallization of saturated-fat-rich neonatal adipose tissue
Cold-induced panniculitis from direct ice crystal formation within subcutaneous tissue
questions.exp: Sclerema neonatorum results from the unique biochemistry of neonatal fat, which contains a very high ratio of saturated fatty acids (palmitic and stearic acids) with a high melting point. In severely ill, premature infants, peripheral circulatory collapse and hypothermia drop skin temperature below the melting point of this fat, while immature lipolytic mechanisms prevent fat mobilization for heat. This causes rapid, widespread crystallization and solidification of subcutaneous adipose tissue, producing the pathognomonic doubly refractile crystals seen on histology.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 4] Sclerema neonatorum vs Subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl with Turner syndrome develops multiple asymptomatic halos around melanocytic nevi on her trunk. She is found to carry the HLA-CW6 allele. Which additional autoimmune condition MOST commonly co-occurs with halo nevi and shares the same CXCL10–CXCR3–driven pathogenic mechanism?
opts: Psoriasis vulgaris mediated by Th17 cells and IL-17
Vitiligo, occurring in approximately 20% of halo nevus patients
Pemphigus vulgaris due to anti-desmoglein-3 autoantibodies
Lichen planus driven by lichenoid CD8+ infiltration of the dermal-epidermal junction
questions.exp:
Vitiligo is the most powerfully associated autoimmune condition with halo nevi, occurring in ~20% of halo nevus patients. Both conditions are mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes targeting melanocytic antigens and share the identical CXCL10–CXCR3 chemokine axis. Turner syndrome itself shows a marked increased frequency of halo nevi (18% vs 1% in controls), linked to HLA-CW6 allele association, highlighting the shared immunogenetic substrate.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a VITILIGO VAMPIRE (20% of castle residents) holding a GLOWING CXCL10–CXCR3 SCEPTER, stalking MELANOCYTE SERVANTS in both the HALO TOWER and the PIGMENT PALACE—two rooms sharing the same IMMUNE TUNNEL.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl presents with sharply demarcated, symmetrically distributed erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales on her extensor surfaces and scalp. Histology shows marked epidermal acanthosis with regular elongation of rete ridges, absent granular layer, and collections of neutrophils in the stratum corneum. Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with her early-onset disease?
opts: HLA-B27
HLA-Cw6 (HLA-C*06:02)
HLA-DR4
HLA-A2
questions.exp: Early-onset plaque psoriasis (Type I) in children is almost invariably associated with the HLA-Cw6 allele within the PSORS1 locus on chromosome 6p21. This strong genetic association distinguishes Type I from late-onset psoriasis and is crucial for disease prognosis and counseling.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: A 6-year-old CHILD kneels before the CASTLE GATE (6p21) where HLA-CW6 guards—imagine the number 6 repeated: chromosome 6, age 6, HLA-Cw6—all gates lead to EARLY childhood psoriasis.

questions.q: An outbreak of severe hand-foot-and-mouth disease with brainstem encephalitis, aseptic meningitis, and acute flaccid paralysis is reported in a pediatric hospital in Singapore. Which pathogen is most likely responsible for this severe neurological presentation?
opts: Coxsackievirus A16
Coxsackievirus B3
Enterovirus 71
Echovirus 11
questions.exp: Enterovirus 71 (EV-A71) is the highly virulent pathogen responsible for severe neurological complications of HFMD, including brainstem encephalitis, encephalomyelitis, aseptic meningitis, and polio-like acute flaccid paralysis. This variant has caused recurrent massive epidemics in the Asia-Pacific region since the late 1990s, with highest mortality in children under 5 years.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: An evil VIRUS-71 EMPEROR sits atop a BRAIN THRONE in an ASIAN CASTLE, commanding brainstem warriors to attack with paralysis and pulmonary floods — EV71's CNS tropism crowns it as the deadly neurologic destroyer.

questions.q: A 7-month-old with severe diaper dermatitis develops multiple reddish-purplish nodules (0.5–3 cm) over the diaper area convexities. Histopathology reveals a dense mixed dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
opts: Jacquet's erosive diaper dermatitis with true granulomatous inflammation
Granuloma gluteale infantum, despite the name lacking true histological granulomas
Atopic dermatitis with secondary bacterial superinfection
Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the intertriginous region
questions.exp: Granuloma gluteale infantum (infantile gluteal granuloma) is a severe irritant variant presenting with violaceous nodules over convex diaper areas. Despite its eponymous name, histology definitively shows NO true granulomas but instead reveals a dense mixed dermal infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils—a hyperplastic tissue reaction to irritants, Candida, or potent corticosteroid misuse.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: A GRANDIOSE NAMING LIE—the castle is called 'GRANULOMA HALL' but ZERO true granulomas live there! Instead, it's a ROWDY PARTY of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils doing the tango in the dermis—false advertising since 1850!

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with a mild febrile illness and a generalised erythematous scarlatiniform rash that spreads rapidly over the body, followed by fine flaky desquamation. The child notably lacks severe pharyngitis and strawberry tongue. Which historical diagnosis would this clinical presentation have been classified under in early 20th-century medicine?
opts: First disease (Measles)
Fourth disease (Filatov-Dukes disease)
Fifth disease (Erythema infectiosum)
Sixth disease (Roseola infantum)
questions.exp: This clinical presentation—a scarlatiniform rash with absent severe pharyngitis and no strawberry tongue—exactly mirrors Clement Dukes' original 1900 description of 4th disease, which he proposed as a distinct exanthem bridging scarlet fever and rubella. Modern medicine now recognises this as an obsolete diagnosis, likely representing staphylococcal scarlatiniform erythroderma or atypical viral exanthems rather than a true distinct disease entity.

questions.q: A 3-week-old female neonate presents with recurrent crops of tense vesicles and bullae in a linear, whorled distribution favoring the extremities and trunk. Which genetic defect and molecular pathway dysfunction best explains the pathogenesis of incontinentia pigmenti?
opts: Mutation in IKBKG gene leading to failure of NF-κB pathway activation and inability to protect keratinocytes from TNF-α-induced apoptosis
Autosomal recessive inheritance with defective desmoglein-3 causing loss of cell-cell adhesion
X-linked recessive WASP gene mutation resulting in immunodeficiency and secondary skin infection
Dominant mutation in KRT14 encoding keratin 14 with structural instability of the basal epidermis
questions.exp: Incontinentia pigmenti is caused by mutations in the IKBKG gene (formerly NEMO), which encodes a regulatory component essential for NF-κB pathway activation. Loss of NF-κB signaling prevents protection of keratinocytes against TNF-α-induced apoptosis, resulting in targeted cell death that follows Blaschko lines due to X-chromosome lyonization. This is NOT an autoimmune or immunobullous disorder, distinguishing it from pemphigus and pemphigoid variants.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: NEMO (the fish) gets STUCK in the NF-κB castle hallway—keratinocytes can't escape TNF-α sharks and DIE in LINEAR BLASCHKO PATTERNS, like the fish swimming in wavering ocean currents.

questions.q: A 6-month-old girl with a history of neonatal vesiculobullous eruption now presents with verrucous, hyperkeratotic papules and plaques in a linear distribution along Blaschko lines. Histopathology from the neonatal stage showed eosinophilic spongiosis with dyskeratotic keratinocytes and marked peripheral eosinophilia. Which stage of incontinentia pigmenti is she most likely entering?
opts: Stage 1 (vesicular stage), which typically persists until 12 months of age
Stage 2 (verrucous/hyperkeratotic stage), representing the natural progression following resolution of blistering
Stage 3 (hyperpigmented stage), indicating successful epidermal remodeling
Stage 4 (atrophic/hypopigmented stage), representing late scarring and involution
questions.exp: Incontinentia pigmenti progresses through four overlapping stages. Stage 1 (vesicular) typically resolves by 4–6 months of age. Stage 2 (verrucous/hyperkeratotic) arises between 2 weeks and 8 weeks of life and follows the resolution of blistering, presenting with warty, hyperkeratotic papules and plaques in the same Blaschko distribution. At 6 months of age with resolved blistering and new verrucous lesions, the patient is entering Stage 2.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Stage 1 BLISTERS burst like BUBBLES in the moat (0–6 months), then Stage 2 WARTS sprout like CASTLE TURRETS on the ramparts (2–8 weeks onward)—the verrucae are HYPERKERATOTIC sentries guarding Blaschko lines.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with a poorly demarcated reddish-blue dermal plaque on the elbow with associated hypertrichosis. Histology shows nodules of spindle-shaped endothelial cells in the mid to deep dermis. According to current ISSVA classification, how does this lesion relate to kaposiform haemangioendothelioma?
opts: It is a distinct, unrelated benign entity with no shared pathogenic mechanism
It represents the superficial, mild end of the same biological spectrum as KHE, sharing identical immunophenotype and capacity for Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon
It is an involuting variant of KHE that has undergone spontaneous regression
It is a GLUT1-positive infantile haemangioma misdiagnosed on histology
questions.exp: Tufted angioma (also called angioblastoma of Nakagawa) is now understood to occupy the superficial, indolent end of a continuous biological spectrum with KHE, sharing identical inappropriate endothelial proliferation, the same immunophenotype, and crucially, the unique capacity to trigger Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon. This unifying concept is supported by overlapping histology and clinical behaviour, distinguishing both from GLUT1-positive infantile haemangiomas which never cause KMP.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 3] Kaposiform Haemangioendothelioma and Tufted Angioma

questions.q: A 9-month-old infant presents with erythematous, edematous dermatitis with scaling and papules affecting the buttocks, lower abdomen, and medial thighs. The deep inguinal folds and gluteal cleft are notably spared. Which of the following best explains the characteristic sparing of intertriginous areas in primary irritant diaper dermatitis?
opts: Autoimmune suppression in the gluteal cleft prevents inflammation
The convex surfaces are in direct contact with the diaper, while intertriginous areas have reduced friction and occlusion
HLA-associated genetic protection in the inguinal region
Candida species preferentially colonize convex surfaces, protecting fold areas
questions.exp: Primary irritant diaper dermatitis characteristically affects convex surfaces (buttocks, abdomen, medial thighs, genitalia) in direct contact with the diaper, while sparing deep inguinal folds and the gluteal cleft. This distribution reflects the pattern of frictional contact and chemical irritation from urine and feces. The intertriginous areas, being deeper and less directly exposed to the irritating elements, remain relatively protected.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CONVEX DOME CASTLE roof getting HAMMERED by rain (diaper irritants), while the DEEP DUNGEON MOAT below stays DRY and SPARED—friction loves the peaks, not the valleys!

questions.q: A 6-year-old immunocompetent child presents with a pruritic rash that started on the face and scalp 2 days ago and has now spread to the trunk. On examination, you observe macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts simultaneously present in the same body area. Which viral receptor is primarily responsible for VZV entry into host cells?
opts: Heparan sulphate proteoglycans and cation-independent mannose 6-phosphate receptor (MPRci)
CD4 receptor and CCR5 co-receptor
ACE2 receptor
Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
questions.exp:
VZV gains cellular entry through multiple receptors including cation-independent mannose 6-phosphate receptor (MPRci), insulin degrading enzyme (IDE), and heparan sulphate proteoglycans. The virus binds these receptors via its envelope glycoproteins (gB, gH, gE, gI). The simultaneous presence of lesions in all stages of development is the single most diagnostic hallmark of classic varicella.
🏰 Palace: Walk through a grand castle entrance labeled 'MPRci DOOR' where a VZV vampire with envelope gB-gH-gI keys simultaneously unlocks heparan-sulfate gates and mannose-phosphate locks to invade the Malpighian layer kingdom.

questions.q: Which clinical feature most reliably distinguishes classic pityriasis lichenoides chronica (Juliusberg disease) from pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta (PLEVA)?
opts: Presence of central micaceous scale on papules
Absence of scarring and post-inflammatory pigmentary changes
Localization to trunk and proximal extremities sparing palms and soles
Chronicity lasting months with minimal systemic symptoms
questions.exp: While PLC does have the pathognomonic micaceous scale and favors trunk/proximal extremities, the CRITICAL distinguishing feature is the ABSENCE of scarring. PLEVA characteristically produces varioliform (chickenpox-like) depressed scars due to severe epidermal necrosis, whereas PLC resolves with only post-inflammatory pigmentary changes. This scarring distinction is the key clinical differentiator between the two ends of the lichenoides spectrum.

questions.q: Which histopathological sign is pathognomonic for lichen nitidus and distinguishes it from other lichenoid dermatoses?
opts: Saw-tooth pattern of epidermal hyperplasia with dense lymphocytic band-like infiltrate obscuring the dermal-epidermal junction
"Ball and claw" sign: dense circumscribed infiltrate (ball) in papillary dermis with elongated rete ridges curving inward to embrace it
Subepidermal cleft with fibrin deposition and acantholytic cells
Epidermal necrosis with interface dermatitis and melanin incontinence
questions.exp: The "ball and claw" sign is the pathognomonic histological hallmark of lichen nitidus, consisting of a well-circumscribed dense infiltrate of lymphocytes and epithelioid histiocytes (the "ball") in the papillary dermis, with adjacent epidermal rete ridges curved inward to laterally embrace the infiltrate (the "claw"). This microscopic appearance is unique and diagnostic, setting lichen nitidus apart from lichen planus and other lichenoid conditions.
questions.memory_hook: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CLAW-HAND sculpture in the castle museum CLUTCHING a CRYSTAL BALL (dense dermal infiltrate) while epidermal FINGERS curve protectively around it—only lichen nitidus has this bizarre 'claw-and-ball' dance!

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 4-month history of small, red-brown, oval papules on his trunk and arms. Each lesion is topped with a tightly adherent scale that, when scraped off, reveals a shining brown surface beneath. Histopathology shows superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with focal parakeratosis and exocytosis forming pseudo-Munro abscesses. Which immune mechanism is primarily responsible for this clinical presentation?
opts: CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell-mediated response with massive epidermal necrosis
Humoral autoimmune response with circulating pathogenic autoantibodies against dermal autoantigens
CD4+ helper T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity with potential FoxP3+ regulatory T-cell involvement
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation with allergic vasculitis
questions.exp: Pityriasis lichenoides chronica is driven by cellular immunity, NOT autoantibodies. The infiltrate is predominantly CD4+ helper T-cells (unlike PLEVA which is CD8+), with some FoxP3+ regulatory T-cells explaining the indolent nature. The mild histology with minimal epidermal necrosis and no massive RBC extravasation further confirms this is a CD4+ response, not the severe CD8+ cytotoxicity seen in acute PLEVA.

questions.q: A 3-month-old male infant with a congenital haemangioma shows persistence of the lesion at near-baseline size with proportionate growth matching his overall body growth. No spontaneous involution has occurred. Which histopathological finding would differentiate this lesion from infantile haemangioma?
opts: Positive GLUT1 immunostaining on endothelial cells
Negative GLUT1 immunostaining on endothelial cells
Presence of BRAF V600E mutation
Absence of somatic mutations in G-protein genes
questions.exp: The cardinal distinguishing feature of congenital haemangiomas (regardless of subtype—RICH, NICH, or PICH) is their universal negativity for GLUT1, the glucose transporter-1 protein. This contrasts sharply with infantile haemangiomas, which are characteristically GLUT1-positive. GLUT1 negativity combined with full size at birth and lack of postnatal proliferation defines congenital haemangiomas.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy with plaque psoriasis develops new lesions at sites of minor skin trauma on his arms after playing outside. His mother also notes he has unusually prominent facial involvement affecting the eyelids. Which pathognomonic histological feature would be MOST characteristic of his lesions when examined under the microscope?
opts: Basilar layer melanin deposition with lichenoid infiltrate
Munro microabscesses and spongiform pustules of Kogoj
Dermal fibrosis with perivascular plasma cell infiltrate
Wedge-shaped parakeratosis overlying a normal granular layer
questions.exp: Munro microabscesses (localized neutrophil collections in the stratum corneum) and spongiform pustules of Kogoj (in the upper spinous layer) are the absolute pathognomonic histological features of psoriasis. These distinguish psoriasis from other inflammatory dermatoses and are present in fully developed lesions regardless of clinical variant.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: MUNRO (Scottish warrior) guards the STRATUM CORNEUM with tiny SWORD-POINT abscesses, while KOGOJ the giant SPONGIFORM guard controls the upper spinous layer—two sentinel fortifications of the psoriasis castle.

questions.q: A 3-month-old infant presents with a deep, poorly demarcated violaceous plaque on the neck that has rapidly enlarged over 6 weeks. Laboratory studies reveal thrombocytopenia (platelets 45,000/μL), elevated D-dimer, and prolonged PT/aPTT. Which vascular tumour diagnosis best explains this clinical constellation?
opts: Infantile haemangioma (GLUT1-positive)
Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma
Congenital haemangioma (RICH type)
Pyogenic granuloma
questions.exp: Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma (KHE) is the classic cause of Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon (KMP)—a life-threatening consumptive coagulopathy characterised by thrombocytopenia, prolonged coagulation times, and elevated D-dimer. Infantile haemangiomas, despite their frequency, never cause KMP, making this the critical differentiating feature. GLUT1-positive infantile haemangiomas lack the shared immunophenotype and biological capacity to trigger KMP that defines both KHE and tufted angioma.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 3] Kaposiform Haemangioendothelioma and Tufted Angioma

questions.q: A 4-year-old child with molluscum contagiosum develops an eczematous inflammatory halo around several lesions without evidence of bacterial superinfection. The parent is concerned this indicates disease progression. Which mechanism best explains this finding?
opts: Secondary bacterial infection requiring topical antibiotics
Spread of infection to deeper dermal layers
A robust host immune response involving cytotoxic T lymphocytes that frequently precedes spontaneous resolution
Transformation to the atypical immunosuppression-associated variant
questions.exp: The inflammatory halo surrounding molluscum lesions represents Meyerson's phenomenon, a manifestation of the host's immune response rather than infection or complications. This inflammatory response, mediated by plasmacytoid dendritic cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes, typically precedes viral clearance and spontaneous resolution.

questions.q: A 9-year-old boy presents with multiple pinhead-sized, shiny, skin-colored papules on the flexor aspects of his forearms and genitalia. Skin biopsy shows a dense, well-circumscribed lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the papillary dermis with elongated epidermal rete ridges curving inward to embrace the infiltrate. Direct immunofluorescence is negative. Which cellular marker would be predominantly elevated in the dermal infiltrate?
opts: CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes
CD4+ helper T-lymphocytes, CD1a+ Langerhans cells, and CD68+ macrophages
IgG-secreting plasma cells
CD20+ B-lymphocytes and anti-desmoglein-3 autoantibodies
questions.exp: Lichen nitidus is a cell-mediated inflammatory condition dominated by CD4+ helper T-lymphocytes, CD1a+/S100+ Langerhans cells, and CD68+/CD14+ macrophages/histiocytes, which polarize toward Th2 immune response. This contrasts sharply with lichen planus, which is CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell predominant, and pemphigus vulgaris, which is antibody-mediated. Direct immunofluorescence is negative because there are no pathogenic autoantibodies involved.
questions.memory_hook: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a CD4+ HELPER KING on a THRONE in the papillary dermis BALLROOM, surrounded by LANGHANS-wearing GUARDS (Langerhans cells) and MACRO-HISTORIANS (macrophages), all dancing the TH2 tango—NO antibody guests allowed (DIF negative)!

questions.q: A premature neonate born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid presents at birth with lethargy, hepatosplenomegaly, and a generalized eruption of discrete grey-white papules and pustules (1-2 mm diameter) with red margins, predominantly on the back. Which organism and pathogenic mechanism best explain these cutaneous findings?
opts: Listeria monocytogenes utilizing internalin A to invade host cells, causing miliary granulomas and microabscesses in the dermis
Streptococcus agalactiae with toxin-mediated epidermal necrosis and subcorneal acantholysis
Candida albicans with pseudohyphae invading the stratum corneum and superficial dermis
Varicella-zoster virus with intranuclear inclusions and ballooning degeneration of keratinocytes
questions.exp: Early-onset neonatal listeriosis (granulomatosis infantiseptica) results from transplacental in utero infection by Listeria monocytogenes, which uses internalin A to invade non-phagocytic cells. Histopathology shows focal tissue necrosis, neutrophilic infiltrates, and monocytes around dermal blood vessels with characteristic miliary granulomas and microabscesses in visceral tissues. The clinical presentation of discrete pustules with red margins in a severely ill premature neonate with meconium-stained fluid is pathognomonic.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with fever, painful oral ulcers on the buccal mucosa and hard palate, followed by characteristic vesicles on the palms and soles. The vesicles are described as elliptical with long axes parallel to skin lines. A skin biopsy is performed. Which of the following findings would help differentiate this condition from herpes simplex virus infection?
opts: Presence of multinucleated giant cells in the epidermis
Intraepidermal vesicles with vacuolar degeneration of keratinocytes but absent viral inclusion bodies and multinucleated giant cells
Subepidermal blistering with dense lymphocytic infiltrate
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis with prominent neutrophilic exudate
questions.exp: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD) demonstrates intraepidermal vesiculation with keratinocyte necrosis but crucially lacks viral inclusion bodies and multinucleated giant cells, which are characteristic of herpes simplex virus and varicella. This histological distinction is key to differentiating HFMD from other viral exanthems.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a HAND holding a FOOT in a MOUTH-shaped castle room with EMPTY shelves (no inclusions/no giant cells) — emphasizing what's MISSING is the diagnostic clue that separates it from herpes's crowded shelves of viral passengers.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child previously vaccinated with a single dose of varicella vaccine 18 months ago now presents with fever and a rash. The rash consists predominantly of 45 maculopapular lesions on the trunk and face with minimal systemic symptoms. Which term best describes this clinical presentation?
opts: Varicella bullosa
Breakthrough varicella (modified varicella)
Classic uncomplicated varicella
Severe atypical varicella
questions.exp:
Breakthrough varicella occurs in 10–15% of patients immunized with a single vaccine dose when exposed to wild-type VZV. The disease is significantly attenuated with predominantly maculopapular (rather than vesicular) lesions, fewer than 60 total lesions, and greatly reduced or absent systemic symptoms like fever. This presentation contrasts with classic varicella, which features rapid evolution to clear vesicles with simultaneous multi-stage lesions and prominent systemic symptoms.
🏰 Palace: Imagine a 'BREAK-THROUGH' castle wall that's been partially reinforced by ONE vaccine guard—the invading VZV army gets stopped early, causing only a MACULOPAPULAR skirmish with <60 soldiers and NO FEVER FIRE.

questions.q: A 14-year-old boy presents with multiple lesions on his upper back, each consisting of a central brown nevus surrounded by a sharply demarcated zone of depigmented skin. Histopathology shows dense band-like infiltrates of CD8+ lymphocytes in the papillary dermis with complete absence of epidermal melanocytes in the surrounding halo zone. Which immunological mechanism MOST accurately explains the pathogenesis of this lesion?
opts: Structural genetic abnormality in melanocyte development during embryogenesis
CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-mediated destruction of melanocytes driven by CXCL10–CXCR3 axis
Inherited melanocytic hamartoma unrelated to autoimmune activation
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation causing epidermal damage
questions.exp:
Halo nevi are fundamentally active, cell-mediated autoimmune processes directed against melanocytic antigens, NOT structural hamartomas. The pathognomonic CD8+ lymphocytic infiltration targets shared melanocytic antigens via the interferon-gamma–inducible CXCL10–CXCR3 chemokine axis, the same mechanism implicated in vitiligo. Circulating anti-melanoma antibodies and cytotoxic isolated lymphocytes further confirm this targeted immunological cascade.
🏰 Palace: Picture a CASTLE UNDER SIEGE (CD8+ troops) storming the BROWN TOWER (nevus) with GLOWING ARROWS (CXCL10–CXCR3) labeled '595nm', leaving a WHITE MOAT (depigmentation) of destroyed melanocytes around the perimeter.

questions.q: A full-term, previously healthy 4-week-old infant presents with fever, irritability, and neck stiffness. CSF analysis confirms bacterial meningitis. Which statement best differentiates late-onset neonatal listeriosis from the early-onset variant?
opts: Late-onset disease targets the CNS and meninges with minimal to no cutaneous involvement, whereas early-onset disease causes widespread petechial and pustular eruptions
Late-onset disease is acquired transplacentally in utero, whereas early-onset disease is acquired during birth canal passage
Late-onset disease presents within the first 48 hours of life, whereas early-onset disease presents several weeks later
Late-onset disease predominantly affects premature and growth-restricted neonates, whereas early-onset disease affects healthy full-term infants
questions.exp: Late-onset listeriosis typically presents as meningitis or meningoencephalitis in healthy full-term infants several weeks after birth, acquired during passage through an infected birth canal or postnatally. Crucially, the skin is generally NOT involved in late-onset disease. In contrast, early-onset disease (granulomatosis infantiseptica) affects premature neonates with severe cutaneous involvement including petechiae, purpura, and pathognomonic grey-white papules with red margins.

questions.q: A neonatologist is comparing two rare adipose tissue disorders in newborns. Sclerema neonatorum (SN) and subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn (SCFN) both present with subcutaneous hardening. However, they differ fundamentally in their classification and underlying pathophysiology. Which of the following correctly categorizes sclerema neonatorum within dermatopathological panniculitis classification and identifies its defining pathological feature?
opts: Septal panniculitis with prominent vasculitis; characterized by acute inflammatory infiltration of blood vessel walls
Lobular panniculitis without vasculitis (disorder of altered fat composition); characterized by fat necrosis with minimal inflammation and radially arranged needle-shaped crystalline clefts
Lymphocytic panniculitis with granuloma formation; characterized by epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans giant cells
Lipoatrophic panniculitis; characterized by progressive loss of subcutaneous fat with autoimmune infiltration
questions.exp: Sclerema neonatorum is classified as a lobular panniculitis without vasculitis, specifically a disorder of altered fat composition rather than inflammatory cell infiltration. The hallmark histological feature is fat necrosis with a striking absence or sparse inflammatory infiltrate, combined with pathognomonic doubly refractile, needle-shaped clefts (representing dissolved triglyceride crystals) arranged radially within adipocytes and thickened connective tissue septa.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 4] Sclerema neonatorum vs Subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn

questions.q: A 2-week-old female infant presents with a firm, fully formed red-violaceous nodule on her left forearm, noted since birth. Immunohistochemistry shows the lesion is negative for GLUT1. Genetic testing reveals a somatic GNAQ Gln209 mutation. Which classification is MOST likely if the lesion begins rapid regression within the first month of life?
opts: Infantile haemangioma
Rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma (RICH)
Non-involuting congenital haemangioma (NICH)
Partially involuting congenital haemangioma (PICH)
questions.exp: Congenital haemangiomas are fully formed at birth (unlike infantile haemangiomas which develop postnatally) and are GLUT1-negative. The GNAQ Gln209 mutation drives all three subtypes. RICH specifically demonstrates rapid postnatal regression beginning within days to weeks and is usually complete by 14 months. The early regression timeline is pathognomonic for RICH.

questions.q: Modern infectious disease experts now attribute the historical cases of Filatov-Dukes disease (4th disease) to misdiagnosis of two main conditions. Which of the following pairs correctly identifies these modern pathological explanations?
opts: Varicella-zoster virus infection and cytomegalovirus reactivation
Staphylococcal scarlatiniform erythroderma (toxin-mediated superantigen response) and atypical viral exanthems (rubella or enterovirus infections)
Group A Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome and invasive meningococcal disease
Acute HIV exanthem and secondary syphilis
questions.exp: The note explains that 4th disease was not a genuine distinct entity but rather cases of Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin-mediated scarlatiniform rash (lacking severe pharyngitis) or mild rubella/enterovirus presentations—both of which clinically mimicked Dukes' original description but had established molecular identities. This distinction is crucial because it explains why the strawberry tongue was absent, unlike true streptococcal scarlet fever.
